items.title: Johnny Wiggs Interview, 1969-12-14
items.q: I don't know whether you know Leo Feist. I've heard up in New York. He used to, when I was in New York about 300 years ago, he used to put out, he was the biggest publisher in New York.

ctx.x: Well, he's one of the great New Orleans trombonists, recording, of course, with Johnny in the 50s, and he dates back long before that. One of his prize records from the 20s was made with Johnny Barsdorfer. Oh. And he recorded also with a band that Johnny Wiggs just mentioned, Norman Brownlee's orchestra. And I couldn't begin to talk about Tom Brown's recordings. There's so many of them he recorded in New York. He was up there quite early.

Yeah, he caught it raw. He was on Canal Street. I remember that. It should be known that Tom Brown was the first white man to take jazz out of New Orleans, his band. Oh, yeah. Up to Chicago, yeah. Up to Chicago, yeah. All the way up there, and then on to New York. That's where they call him that dirty old name of a jazz player. Before getting off, I wanted to ask you, since I'm in my 50s, too, I mean, I do a little composing, but I can't adapt to rock and roll. Perhaps I'm too old. But is there any market for…

It's really hard now. The whole music scene has changed so much. That's right. Okay, we certainly do appreciate your comments. Thank you. Nice talking to you. Thank you for calling. Let's talk it over and talking it over with Johnny Wiggs of Johnny Wiggs and his New Orleans Kings and Mr. Dick Allen of Tulane University's Jazz Archives. The number to call? All, well, yeah, 523-2404. There's one line open, the one we've just vacated, but it won't be open very long, I should imagine. You've heard of the Industrial…
